articles.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
articles.summary: Websites were taken offline after the developers of programming language PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" had been discovered.
articles.body:
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.

Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.

There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.

Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.

"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.

She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".

The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".

"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.

Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".

"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.

But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.

He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected had been received and was being acted on.

Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb

What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?

Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.

"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.

"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."

Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.

He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.

"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.

He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.

PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.

It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.

When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.

It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.

According to cyber-security firm Wiz , which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.

And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.

Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.

Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.

While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.

The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.

But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.

In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.

"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.

"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."

Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.

"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".

"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

articles.title: In 2023, Olivia Wilde bought a four-bedroom Los Angeles home for $5.9 million; the 0.66-acre property sold in December 2025 for $5.23 million, about $670,000 below what she paid
articles.summary: Olivia Wilde has sold her sprawling Studio City home in Los Angeles for $5.23 million, according to a report by Realtor.com.
articles.body: Olivia Wilde has sold her sprawling Studio City home in Los Angeles for $5.23 million, according to a report by Realtor.com. The sale closed in December 2025 for about $670,000 less than she paid when she purchased the property in 2023. The sale came amid speculation about her romance with British art dealer Caspar Jopling. Perhaps all is fair in love!A 1947 homeThe original house was built in 1947 and has been remodelled over the decades. Architect Barbara Bestor designed the Sunswept House, while Swike carried out its more recent refresh in 2015, and Judy Kameon of Elysian Landscapes designed the gardens. The property was described in its Redfin listing as “an exceptionally private modern-ranch retreat”. The house is set on more than half an acre.Inside the house and the yardThe home has an open floor plan and opens into a bright main space where the living room, dining area and kitchen flow together. Large glass doors slide into the walls and open onto a dining terrace, a lounge and a separate outdoor kitchen, making the indoors and outdoors feel like one area. The kitchen is built around a large island. The listing describes the home as ‘quintessentially Californian’. “This is indoor-outdoor living at its best.” The home receives abundant natural light, thanks to the skylights and wide windows. The main bedroom has a large closet and its own bathroom, as well as glass doors that look out onto the garden. A cedar soaking tub and an outdoor shower sit just outside. The opposite wood-panelled wing houses three guest bedrooms: a private guest suite featuring an en-suite three-quarter bathroom, as well as two additional bedrooms with a shared full bathroom. Downstairs, there is a relaxed living room that could serve as a den, a playroom or a small screening room. Outside, there is a detached guest house with a kitchenette and bathroom, as well as a pool house with a sauna. The grounds also include two vegetable gardens, mature trees and parking for more than six cars. “Sunswept is at once private, pedigreed, and deeply livable – an extraordinary creative compound designed for both entertaining and everyday life, just moments from Erewhon, Equinox, and the best Ventura Boulevard has to offer,” the listing says.Olivia Wilde first listed her Studio City home for $6.2 million in September 2025, less than three months before the sale. The buyer paid $5.23 million, and the sale closed in December 2025. That gap is what makes the sale stand out. Real estate deals often close below the asking price, but a gap this large means the seller took a clear loss on the purchase price she paid.Wilde’s Studio City sale came after the sale of her Silver Lake home. In September 2023, she sold her Silver Lake home for $4.2 million. The actress had bought it with Jason Sudeikis during their relationship, and it went to her in the split. The sale came close to the time the couple finalised their custody arrangement. The former couple began their whirlwind relationship in 2011 after meeting at a Saturday Night Live party. Within a year, they were engaged. The two share time with their children, Otis and Daisy. The couple is focused on co-parenting their two children. “It's been amicable, and they've transitioned into a great co-parenting routine. The children are the priority and the heart of the family's relationship,” an insider told People at the time of the split.Interestingly, Wilde’s decision to sell the Studio City home came amid speculation about her relationship with Caspar Jopling. Speaking to The Cut in June this year, Olivia Wilde spoke about her boyfriend, Caspar Jopling, for the first time. “When you’re with someone who’s not in the entertainment industry or isn’t a public figure, I have a sense of, ‘I want to protect this person as much as I can,’” she told the outlet. “I’m in a really lovely relationship now. I adore him, and I feel completely whole and intact as a person. I think it’s only possible after spending a couple years alone. If you haven’t ever been single for a few years, how do you even know who you are?”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Warren gets defensive when pressed on Democrats accepting billionaire donations
articles.summary: Elizabeth Warren grew defensive when pressed on Michael Bloomberg's $80 million to Democrats, and Troy Jackson's donations from billionaires after railing against them.
articles.body: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., got defensive in a new interview as she railed against billionaire donations in politics and was asked about Democrat Troy Jackson revealing multiple billionaire donors, as well as a large possible donation from Michael Bloomberg. CNN's Kaitlan Collins said during an interview with Warren that Bloomberg had given about $80 million to help Democrats win the midterms after noting that Elon Musk had contributed $276 million to Republicans. Collins asked Warren, "You're someone who has said billionaire donors should not be in politics. Given what you've said, do you want Michael Bloomberg's help here?" THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY – AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES "Look, what I want is to get this kind of money out of politics," Warren said. "Right now, the Republicans know that their only chance, as they see it, to be able to hang on to the House and the Senate and some of these governors' mansions is to be able to just drown people in money, to be able to run all the ads on TV, to lie, to cheat, and that there won't be any opportunity for Democrats to be able to respond." "We need to push back because, this campaign, this 2026 midterm, really is about the money or the people. Because the Democrats have got the people on their side. The Republicans have got the money, and they think if they can spend it, they can maintain control of this country, and I sure hope they're wrong," Warren said, arguing for a "very different" system. Collins then raised Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who said during a debate against his opponent, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, that he had no billionaires funding him. However, a financial report released by the campaign earlier this month found there were at least four billionaire donors funding him, according to Fox23. "Do you think that he needs to address that contradiction?" Collins asked Warren. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' "So look, really? That's where we're going to make the focus? So, Susan Collins has all this money coming in against her. Elon Musk has come in and put, I don't know, what are the numbers now, how many tens of millions of dollars? And we're going to say, ‘Oops, Troy Jackson may have gotten one of his numbers wrong. He may have gotten contributions from four billionaires,’" she responded. She said she wanted all the billionaires out. HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE' "I don't think they ought to be able to control elections," she said. "But understand this: it is the Republicans who are outspending Democrats like crazy. And it's not Republicans who are small-dollar donors. It's billionaires and a trillionaire who think that they can just back up dump truck loads full of money, and they will be able to buy a Senate seat in Maine." She went on to point a finger at President Donald Trump. "That's a big part of why so much is broken in this country. It's that billionaires and insiders for Donald Trump are calling all the shots," she said. Jackson's campaign did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. "Elizabeth Warren and Troy Jackson are both morally bankrupt hypocrites who want power at any cost. Warren overlooked Graham Platner's horrendous history in favor of advancing her socialist agenda, and now she's doing the same with his knock-off replacement," RNC spokesperson Kristen Cianci told Fox News Digital in a statement. Warren was interviewed about her speech at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., at the time, where she said Democrats had to "credibly demonstrate" they could take on a "rigged system," which might mean upsetting the wealthy. In the address, she contrasted Democrats who will take on the fight head-on and those who "politely nibble around the edges of change." "So, look, the Democrats need to build a bigger tent in order to win in 2026, 2028 and beyond. So the question is, how do we do that?" Warren told CNN. While she said he has not managed to follow through, she credited Trump for at least discerning that one of everyday Americans' biggest priorities is wanting basic costs lowered. articles.title: DHS can't knock on the doors and ask people about their immigration status, rules federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge has now ruled that Department of Homeland Security officials can't knock on people's doors to ask about their immigration status and
articles.body: A federal judge has now ruled that Department of Homeland Security officials can't knock on people's doors to ask about their immigration status and whether they have voted in the recent elections, as the action likely violated the Voting Rights Act. The department posted photos and videos of agents carrying out the operation to find out illegitimate voters. In her ruling, US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are US citizens."Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 pm on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek an appeal."Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge, Martinez-Olguin, wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate US citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."The lawsuit was filed by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United, along with the Voto Latino Foundation, San Francisco and Santa Clara County. A request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security was not immediately returned.Homeland Security said in a statement on Thursday that the department is "laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of US citizens." The department added that they have "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be US citizens."Operation Protect the VoteFederal law enforcement recently arrested 11 foreign nationals in California who were among 28 total charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in US elections. The Operation Protect the Vote is a coordinated effort among all four California-based US Attorney's offices to combat and root out fraud n US elections. All 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents or Green Card holders who have legal immigration status in the United States, but are not permitted to vote in US elections.You use AI every day. Eric Lewis, 35, is accused of fatally shooting Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber and wounding his partner. He faces a range of state charges, among them murder, homicide of a law enforcement officer, attempted murder, 10 counts of attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault, terroristic threats and other related offenses. He is certainly not allowed to steal a firearm, and under federal law, he is certainly prohibited from using any firearm to rob, shoot, and kill a police officer, as a result of those actions," Metcalf said. "No one attacks law enforcement without facing the consequences," he said when the new federal charges were announced. SUSPECT IN DEADLY PHILADELPHIA POLICE AMBUSH FACES 76 CHARGES, ORDERED HELD WITHOUT BAIL The wounded officer, Hector Rodriguez III, who remains hospitalized but in stable condition, was shot 12 times. articles.title: In 2026, Rhino Boy Chris ran 132 marathons in one rhino suit and raised more than £50,000 for rhino conservation, setting a Guinness record along the way
articles.summary: In April 2026, Chris Green, known as Rhino Boy, ran 132 marathons in a rhino suit, setting a Guinness World Record and raising over £50,000 for rhino conservation. His efforts highlight the importance of wildlife protection and community awareness.
articles.body: Chris Green, popularly known as the Rhino Boy, crossed the finish line of his 200th marathon at the TCS London Marathon in April 2026 and individually completed 132 in costume. This earned him recognition from Guinness World Records as the record holder for the most marathons completed in the same three-dimensional costume by a male participant. According to a 2026 London Marathon update, Green’s campaign as a marathon runner has raised more than £50,000 for Save the Rhino International.From marathon running to a conservation campaignGreen’s record was a result of his tireless effort of running in the same rhino costume, and The Green Runners reported last year that in April 2025, Green had already started his preparation for his 113th Marathon run at the London Marathon, leaving 19 more to go. By then, Green already held the Guinness World Record as the fastest marathoner in a mammal costume when he completed the 2021 London Marathon in 4 hours, 6 minutes and 35 seconds.His endeavours as a marathoner have taken him places beyond the track; Green even climbed Mount Kilimanjaro earlier this year as an effort to raise awareness for rhinos under threat and generate support for conservation. Save the Rhino International said the challenge kept alive a tradition tied to the costume, which harks back to 1994, when the first conservation expedition summited the mountain alongside the charity’s founders, Douglas Adams and Kenyan conservationist Michael Werikhe.Green’s conservation efforts have also been translated from track into literary work, having authored a children’s book called Matumaini, The Rhinos’ Hope. The book focuses on a rhino as its central character, and the name Matumaini, which originates from Swahili, translates to “hope”. Green’s intention in writing the book was to use the sales alongside donations to benefit Save the Rhino International, which he revealed on his fundraising page. The charity focuses on supporting conservation projects across Africa and Asia by engaging with local communities and rangers; it seeks to establish rhino populations and address habitat loss.Taking rhino conservation into the communityGreen joined The Green Runners, an organisation with the objective of making marathon running as a sport more environmentally responsible. Speaking in an interview conducted in 2025 with the outlet, he opened on the challenges of reconciling his conservation efforts with the toll of environmental costs, long-distance flights and driving trucks as a profession. “I also work in removals, and I have to drive trucks. I see the good in moving people – both physically and emotionally, in their lives, but if I had my way I’d be a full-time rhino!”The same report noted Green hosted five school visits in April 2025 to educate children about the plight of rhinos, while his effort to hold conversations with the public remains an ongoing project. Green, who donned his moniker as the Rhino Boy, was among the 59,830 athletes who finished the race, and the event, as per estimates from the Olympics, raised an amount above £95 million. Green’s 132-marathon record was confirmed by Guinness World Records, while Save the Rhino International reported that his fundraising had passed £50,000 by April 2026.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI/SRINAGAR: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk accused Centre of backtracking on an understanding reached with Ladakh groups in May 2026, including on a UT-level elected body, calling the failure to hold talks in Delhi on Thursday “yet another betrayal of trust”. “The govt had said Ladakh lacked resources for full statehood. Instead, it is talking about a small council, which is shameful and undignified for Ladakh,” he said.Raising the bar, Wangchuk said, “We are now saying that Ladakh should be granted full statehood.” This would send out a message to China and the rest of the world, he added.LAB and KDA representatives had prepared for Oct 22 talks after an Oct 15 meeting in Leh, expecting discussion of drafts on the powers of the UT-level body and district councils. Wangchuk alleged the Ladakh administration was making decisions unilaterally and curtailing district councils’ powers.Meanwhile, a Civil Society Forum of Ladakh convention accused LAB and KDA of rejecting MHA’s draft proposal without examination. Led by former MP Thupstan Chhewang, it blamed cancellation on “misinformation and disregard for consensus” by LAB and KDA leaders. articles.title: In 2019, an Ohio engineer bought 34 wooded acres and began building unusual vacation rentals; five years later, his three-property business reported more than $700,000 in yearly revenue and $350,000 in net profit
articles.summary: An Ohio engineer’s decision to trade a conventional career for an unconventional hospitality business has turned a wooded property in Hocking Hills into a
articles.body: An Ohio engineer’s decision to trade a conventional career for an unconventional hospitality business has turned a wooded property in Hocking Hills into a lucrative vacation rental destination. Bryant Gingerich, who founded Dunlap Hollow with his wife, Amy, transformed an old cottage, a contemporary A-frame and a natural cave into distinctive holiday homes. According to Fortune, which reported on the business in January 2025, the three rentals generated more than $700,000 in annual revenue, with net profits exceeding $350,000. The property listings on Airbnb and the business’s official website offer further insight into how the unusual stays have been developed and marketed.From a wooded property to a hospitality businessGingerich’s journey began with a 34-acre parcel in Ohio that offered a combination of rugged terrain, sandstone formations, woodland and natural features. Although he was trained as a mechanical engineer, his interest in construction and design made the land an opportunity to build something beyond his regular professional life.He and Amy acquired the property with financial assistance from family and a local lender. Their first project was an existing cottage that needed extensive renovation before it could welcome guests. The initial rental performed well enough to establish a foundation for the business. That early response encouraged the couple to invest in more ambitious accommodation, eventually creating Dunlap Hollow, a collection of stays designed around the landscape rather than conventional hotel-style rooms.Three distinctive stays with different appealThe business now offers three properties, each catering to travellers looking for a different kind of escape. The Cottage is a renovated one-bedroom home with a loft, combining a rustic setting with contemporary comforts. Surrounded by woodland and sandstone cliffs, it provides a smaller, more intimate option for guests visiting the Hocking Hills region.The A-Frame takes a more architectural approach. Designed with large windows and a striking triangular structure, the three-bedroom property accommodates larger groups and includes amenities such as a hot tub, outdoor fire features and access to private hiking trails. Its design has also attracted interest from people looking to recreate a similar home elsewhere.The most distinctive property is The Cave, a roughly 1,500-square-foot residence built into a natural recess in the rock. Despite its unusual setting, the accommodation includes two bedrooms, bathrooms, a fully equipped kitchen, a luxurious bathtub and modern entertainment facilities. Its interiors contrast the surrounding stone with carefully selected furnishings and decorative details.According to the official Dunlap Hollow website, the properties were designed by Bryant and Amy Gingerich, with additional architectural and interior design support for the A-frame and cave. Their combination of natural surroundings and considered interiors has helped distinguish the rentals in a competitive holiday accommodation market.How social media helped drive demandVisual appeal has been central to Dunlap Hollow’s growth. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional property listings, the business used social media to reach travellers who discover holiday destinations through photographs and videos.The couple initially promoted the A-Frame through complimentary stays offered to influencers in exchange for exposure. As the properties gained visibility, the business attracted a wider audience and developed a following around its distinctive architecture and woodland setting.The strategy helped turn the rentals into destinations in their own right. The official website now supports direct bookings, while the properties remain listed on Airbnb, where guests can review the accommodation, amenities and overall experience. The business has also found a second source of income through the A-Frame’s design. Demand from people interested in building similar homes led Gingerich to offer architectural drawings and computer-aided design plans for sale. Fortune reported that these plans had generated approximately $220,000 in passive income over three years, adding a digital product business to the rental operation.Leaving engineering for a more hands-on careerGingerich left his engineering role in 2020, during the Covid-19 pandemic, as he committed more time to developing Dunlap Hollow. The decision carried financial risk, particularly because the property’s mortgage represented a substantial share of his previous salary. articles.title: At 19, Pat Craig began rescuing captive big cats; today, his Colorado sanctuary spans 10,500 acres and shelters 400+ rescued animals
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of Pat Craig, who founded the Wild Animal Sanctuary in Colorado at just 19, rescuing over 400 big cats and other animals from captivity and giving them a new home in expansive natural habitats.
articles.body: Pat Craig began rescuing captive wild animals in Colorado at the young age of 19, and in 1980, he built his first sanctuary as a small facility on his family’s farm near Boulder. The Wild Animal Sanctuary operates across more than 10,500 acres of natural habitat more than four decades later, and houses more than 400 rescued lions, tigers, bears, wolves, and other animals at its main site near Keenesburg.Craig’s decision came from a visit to a zoo in North Carolina, where a friend showed him that lions and tigers were kept in small cages away from public viewing areas, as they were considered surplus and had no place at the zoo. Deeply troubled by what he had seen, Craig returned to Colorado and began contacting zoos and other facilities to provide homes to animals that might otherwise be euthanised or sold.Craig became the youngest state- and federally licensed zoological director in the country at the time, according to the sanctuary’s official history. He started off with a small compound on the family farm and took in animals from facilities that could no longer keep them, and moved and expanded the operation later as more animals needed space.The sanctuary moved beyond cagesThe rescued animals still lived in concrete enclosures with metal bars at first, according to the regulations that governed the facility. Craig began letting them into larger fenced areas during the day, one at a time, and noticed that the animals often returned to their cages at night, which he interpreted as a sign that familiar spaces could provide a sense of security even when larger habitats were available.The organisation’s habitats give animals more room to move than conventional small cages, while safety was maintained by fences and carefully managed groupings. Staff consider species and individual behaviour before introducing animals to one another, and the sanctuary says that its work has also involved educating the public and government officials about the conditions in which captive wild animals are kept.A 2021 report by The Gazette described the sanctuary’s growth from its founding in 1980 to a facility in Keenesburg that housed more than 400 animals. The site covered about 720 acres at the time, and Craig was continuing to expand the organisation’s land holdings. The report also described how animals that were rescued from zoos, circuses and private ownership were given space to live in habitats rather than small enclosures.A large refuge requires land, food and fundingCraig’s organisation began purchasing a large ranch in southeastern Colorado for a second major facility in 2018, and the expansion included thousands of acres that were intended for large habitats, which gave the sanctuary more room to take in animals. A 2019 report by 5280 described the planned expansion near Springfield, Colorado, and included a 9,004-acre ranch purchase and an additional 680 acres of leased land. The purpose of the new site was to accommodate animals in habitats that were far larger than the cages in which many had previously lived. The report noted that the expansion was designed to increase capacity for rescued lions, tigers and bears.The founder’s page says that the organisation uses around 100,000 pounds of food each week for the animals across its facilities, and also relies on donations and food that was supplied by a national retailer to manage operating costs. Land is only one part of the work, since staff must provide food, veterinary care, secure fencing and suitable habitats for animals with different needs. The organisation now operates multiple facilities in Colorado, including the large Keenesburg sanctuary and its southeastern Colorado refuge, with its stated focus being the rescue of captive wild animals that have been abused, abandoned, exploited, or kept illegally.You use AI every day. articles.title: From 1979 into the early 2000s, Michael Kahn and Leda Livant built Eliphante from found materials, transforming a 3-acre Arizona property into a sculptural desert compound
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating story of Eliphante, a sculptural art environment created by Michael Kahn and Leda Livant using found materials over nearly three decades in Arizona.
articles.body: Michael Kahn and Leda Livant began the construction of Eliphante in 1979 on a three-acre property near Cornville, Arizona. Rocks, driftwood, construction waste, glass, pottery fragments and other salvaged materials were used to build a collection of unusual structures that grew over nearly three decades, and the SPACES Archives records the site as a sculptural environment that was built between 1979 and the early 2000s.The couple were in search of a place where Kahn could paint, so they moved west from Provincetown, Massachusetts, and settled near Oak Creek after meeting landowners who allowed them to stay on part of their property. Their first shelter was a truck, and the rocky landscape that surrounded it soon became part of Kahn’s approach to building. Kahn and Livant started building structures as ideas developed, and used materials that were gathered from the creek, nearby washes and construction sites, and the compound that resulted included domes, curved rooms, passageways, mosaics and a subterranean gallery.The building that gave Eliphante its nameThe first major structure was completed in roughly five years, but the couple never lived in it, and the name Eliphante came because a friend remarked that the building was similar to an elephant because of its trunk-like entrance and irregular roof. Kahn and Livant later built the Hipadome, which became their home, while another major structure, called Pipe Dreams, functioned as an underground gallery, with its interior incorporating mosaics that were made from stained glass and ceramic pieces, along with fabrics and carpet assemblages.Kahn collected rocks from nearby terrain and used driftwood that was deposited by seasonal floods, and the pair also incorporated waste from community construction projects into domes, shelters and other structures. A 2008 profile in The New York Times, titled “A Handmade Home,” described the compound and the couple’s approach to building without conventional architectural plans.A home that became a sculptural environmentKahn had studied at the Art Students League and the National Academy of Design before moving to Arizona, with his expertise in painting and sculpture. The site that he built eventually included more than the elephant-shaped building and the Hipodome, and its separate structures, galleries, and outdoor installations created a network of spaces across the property. Glass, mirrors, pottery shards and other materials became part of both the interiors and exteriors.The couple continued building for almost 30 years, and eventually the structures themselves became part of Kahn’s artistic practice. In 1987, Kahn and Livant started the nonprofit Eliphante Ltd. to help protect the site after their deaths, and in 1994, Eliphante was included in the Smithsonian American Art Museum’s Save Outdoor Sculpture! catalogue.Preservation and public access remain difficultKahn died in December 2007, following which Livant moved off the property in 2009, according to the SPACES Archives, which also notes that Eliphante is a private residence and is not open to the public. The site has faced questions about its long-term condition and access, with Atlas Obscura’s listing stating that Eliphante was permanently closed to visitors.Although photographs and archival records document the buildings, the compound is not a public attraction with routine visitor access, and the structures remain on private property in Cornville, with the nonprofit’s preservation role being separate from a guarantee that the public can enter. Eliphante’s construction spanned the years from 1979 into the early 2000s, and the site’s surviving buildings preserve the couple’s use of found materials and their decision to let the design develop through the work itself.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Charles Schwab, the discount brokerage businessman, found a quiet retreat from his corporate life in Montana’s Bitterroot Valley, where he could enjoy the
articles.body: Charles Schwab, the discount brokerage businessman, found a quiet retreat from his corporate life in Montana’s Bitterroot Valley, where he could enjoy the outdoors, drive along dirt roads, and leave his business suits behind. In the 1990s, he turned his attention to the historic Stock Farm, a 2,600-acre Thoroughbred horse ranch once owned by copper king Marcus Daly.Schwab invested an estimated $30 million in restoring the property and developing a private golf club. The plans included red barns, guest houses, log cabins, and an 18-hole golf course designed by Tom Fazio. According to Forbes, Schwab viewed the project as a personal venture rather than a way to make money, even as golf memberships and land parcels went on sale.Charles Schwab invested around $30 million in Montana’s historic Stock FarmSchwab’s decision to invest in the Stock Farm followed a problem with golfing in the Bitterroot Valley. The public golf course in nearby Hamilton was overcrowded and marked by divots, making it less suitable for his 10-handicap game. He responded by putting an estimated $30 million into the 100-year-old, 2,600-acre property, which had belonged to copper king Marcus Daly and operated as a Thoroughbred horse ranch. Schwab wanted to restore the historic property while creating a private golf destination.Fly-fishing, dirt roads and casual living shaped Charles Schwab’s Montana escapeThe Bitterroot Valley, around 35 miles south of Missoula, provided Schwab with a place to step away from his business responsibilities. At the ranch and in the surrounding area, he adopted a more informal routine, going fly-fishing in waders, wearing jeans and driving a brown-and-white 1980 Chevy Suburban along dirt roads.He also regularly ate supper at Cantina La Cocina, a 20-table restaurant in downtown Victor. Schwab’s description of his clothing reflected his relaxed approach to life in Montana. He said, "I wear the Gap denims since I'm on the board."Red barns and a private golf course formed part of the Stock Farm projectThe restoration plans drew on the ranch’s historic character. Schwab intended to build red barns with galvanised-steel roofs, following the style associated with Daly a century earlier. The club buildings and guest houses were planned with clapboard exteriors and pitched single roofs, alongside log cabins with stone bases.A private golf club was central to the development. Its 18-hole course was designed by Tom Fazio, a prominent golf course designer, and was scheduled to open in the autumn of 1998. The project brought together the restoration of the former horse ranch and the creation of a private recreational facility.Stock Farm offered private golf memberships and luxury land lots for saleThe Stock Farm development also included opportunities to buy memberships in the private golf club and land in the surrounding timber highlands. The club offered 350 memberships. By the time Forbes reported on the project in October 1998, 75 memberships had been sold.The development also offered 96 lots ranging from one to 35 acres. Prices were set between $250,000 and $1 million, although only 12 lots had been purchased at the time of the report.Schwab said, "My life is about investing so this is just a unique thing for me to do.”"It's not about making money."You use AI every day. articles.title: 21 years on, double life term for Jammu terror attack that killed baby, 2 others
articles.summary: JAMMU: A Jammu court has imposed two life sentences and fines of Rs 2 lakh on Mohammed Sharief, a terrorist who gunned down three members of a family,
articles.body: JAMMU: A Jammu court has imposed two life sentences and fines of Rs 2 lakh on Mohammed Sharief, a terrorist who gunned down three members of a family, including a six-month-old infant, in Ramban district’s Gool area over 21 years ago.In his order on Wednesday, principal sessions judge Ramban Ajay Kumar Gupta rejected defence arguments that the attack had taken place more than two decades ago when Sharief was young, his long incarceration and possibility of rehabilitation.Besides the life sentences, the court imposed two separate terms of 10 years on Sharief under various sections pertaining to murder and arms act offences. “All sentences shall run concurrently, while the period already spent in custody shall be set off in accordance with law,” the judge said.The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack and directed J&K State Legal Services Authority to provide compensation to heirs of the deceased and the survivors.Judge Gupta rejected defence arguments about the testimony of two injured eyewitnesses, saying they were reliable and corroborated by medical and other evidence. Defective investigations or delay in recording statements could not automatically result in acquittal when credible evidence otherwise established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the judge said.Public prosecutor Wajid Ahmed pressed for maximum punishment under law, contending that the murder of three innocent family members, including the baby, and the use of an AK-47 rifle warranted a stringent sentence.The court considered aggravating and mitigating circumstances and held that although the crime was extremely grave, the case did not warrant the death penalty under the rarest of rare principle.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Since 2016, South Africa’s Rhino Peak Challenge has raised almost R8 million through a 21-km route to the 3,056-metre summit for wildlife conservation
articles.summary: Join the Rhino Peak Challenge to climb South Africa's 3,056-metre summit while raising funds for wildlife conservation efforts. Discover how this annual event supports endangered species and environmental projects as it celebrates its ongoing success since 2016.
articles.body: The Rhino Peak Challenge asks participants to complete a 21-kilometre mountain route in South Africa’s Maloti-Drakensberg Park, and reach a summit that is located 3,056 metres above sea level. The event began in 2016, and has raised almost R8 million for wildlife conservation, according to its official website.The fundraiser takes place annually and supports projects that are focused on threatened species such as rhinos, vultures and cranes. Participants take on the climb as conservation ambassadors, and also raise money through individual fundraising campaigns and donations. The route can be completed on foot at the participant’s own pace, but the terrain and elevation make it a highly demanding challenge even for hikers who are experienced, as the challenge takes place within the Maloti-Drakensberg Park World Heritage Site, which is a protected mountain landscape that crosses the border between South Africa and Lesotho.A 21-kilometre route to the summitThe challenge covers 21 kilometres to the summit of Rhino Peak and back, and participants can either walk or run, with no time limit. The event organisers say most ambassadors complete the course in four to nine hours, as per their pace and conditions. Rhino Peak rises to 3,056 metres, and the climb takes place in a wilderness area instead of an urban running course, which makes participation limited, with selected ambassadors expected to raise money for the event’s conservation beneficiaries. The official challenge website lists the fastest known times as 2 hours and 15 minutes for men, a record set by Kane Reilly, and 2 hours and 45 minutes for women, set by Holly Page.Where does the fundraising go?The Rhino Peak Challenge directs funds to several conservation organisations such as Wildlife ACT, the Endangered Wildlife Trust and Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, with the event’s current website also listing the Bearded Vulture Recovery Programme. Wildlife ACT works on the monitoring and protection of threatened wildlife in southern Africa, and the organisation says that money that is raised through the challenge supports conservation work involving species such as rhinos, vultures and cranes. The Endangered Wildlife Trust also identifies the fundraiser as a source of support for projects targeting those groups.The beneficiaries address different conservation pressures, including wildlife monitoring and anti-poaching efforts to habitat protection and species recovery, with the funds being allocated to specific projects. Wildlife ACT’s fundraising page confirms the challenge’s launch in 2016 and says that it has raised more than R6 million for its original key beneficiaries. The newer total on the event’s own website is almost R8 million, which reflects a later reporting point.Why the event limits participationThe number of ambassadors is restricted because the route passes through a protected wilderness area, and those who are interested in taking part must apply to become ambassadors, and each participant is expected to commit to fundraising. The organisers set a minimum fundraising commitment of R20,000 for ambassadors, and this format makes fundraising part of the participation requirement, rather than leaving donations entirely to spectators or sponsors.The challenge has continued as an annual event since its launch, and its conservation work depends on the money raised by participants and donors, while access to the mountain route remains limited. The official event website lists the 2026 challenge for September 19 and provides information for prospective ambassadors and donors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A six-story Phoenix office tower dating to 1922 has sold for $10.3 million, and its new owner Aperture Hotels plans to turn the century-old Ellis Building downtown into a Marriott hotel with around 100 rooms
articles.summary: A historic office building in downtown Phoenix is set for a new chapter as the city continues to repurpose older commercial properties for hospitality.
articles.body: A historic office building in downtown Phoenix is set for a new chapter as the city continues to repurpose older commercial properties for hospitality. The Ellis Building, a six-story structure dating to the early 20th century, has been acquired by hotel developer Aperture Hotels, which plans to transform the property into a boutique hotel under Marriott’s Tribute Portfolio brand. According to reporting by The Arizona Republic, published through the USA Today Network, and property information from real estate database Vizzda and brokerage NewGen Advisory, the building sold for $10.3 million, with the transaction closing on October 6, 2026. The redevelopment follows years of unsuccessful attempts to find a viable new use for the historic property.A century-old building finds a new purposeLocated at the intersection of Second Avenue and Monroe Street, the Ellis Building contains approximately 61,000 square feet of space. Constructed in 1922, it originally served as an office building, with two additional floors added in 1928.The property remained associated with city offices for decades before Phoenix sold it to Equus Development Corp. in 2019. Subsequent redevelopment plans sought to adapt the building for modern commercial use, but limited demand for office space and an unfinished residential conversion complicated those efforts. The latest proposal offers a different route to preserving the structure by giving it a hospitality-focused purpose. Phoenix approved plans to convert the building into a hotel in May 2026, paving the way for the transaction and the proposed redevelopment.What the hotel will offerAperture Hotels plans to develop the Ellis Building into a Tribute Portfolio property, part of Marriott International’s collection of independent hotels. The project is expected to include between 95 and 105 guest rooms, alongside a restaurant and bar on the ground floor.The conversion will bring a new hospitality use to a property whose earlier redevelopment plans did not come to fruition. Rather than continuing as traditional office space, the building is expected to become part of downtown Phoenix’s accommodation market, serving visitors seeking a centrally located stay.The Tribute Portfolio designation is significant because the brand focuses on individual properties with distinct identities, allowing historic buildings to retain some of their character while operating within Marriott’s broader hospitality network. The project’s final room count and other operational details may be refined as redevelopment progresses.A wider shift in downtown PhoenixThe Ellis Building is not the only historic downtown office property moving towards hotel use. Phoenix approved a development agreement in August 2026 for the preservation and conversion of the Security Building and Annex Building, another major adaptive-reuse project. Developed by Phoenix-based CivicGroup, the proposed $135 million redevelopment is expected to create a full-service hotel with 255 guest rooms, a 5,500-square-foot ballroom, 13,000 square feet of meeting space, and restaurant and bar facilities.The Security Building was constructed in 1928, while the Annex Building dates to 1961. The Security Building was added to the Phoenix Historic Property Register in 1987. Both properties have been used as offices for Maricopa County, which is consolidating operations and relocating functions to other county-owned sites. Together, the two projects illustrate how older commercial buildings can be considered for new uses as downtown property owners and developers respond to changing demand for office space and hospitality accommodation.Preserving the past while adapting to new demandThe Ellis Building’s planned transformation reflects a broader challenge facing historic urban districts: finding economically viable uses for ageing buildings without losing their architectural and historical significance. Converting an existing structure into a hotel can offer an alternative to leaving a property underused, particularly when previous office or residential plans have stalled. However, the success of such projects depends on the practicalities of adapting older buildings to modern hotel requirements, including guest facilities, circulation and building systems.For Phoenix, the Ellis Building’s sale marks a step towards bringing a long-standing downtown property back into active use. If the redevelopment proceeds as planned, the former office tower will join a growing group of historic buildings being reimagined for visitors, adding another hospitality destination to the city’s urban core.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: RILEY GAINES: Call Her Daddy's advice is a dangerous recipe for lifelong regret
articles.summary: Alex Cooper and Sophia Bush's viral marriage advice sparks a deeper debate about feminism, sacrifice, and what empowerment truly means for women.
articles.body: In a viral exchange this week, Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper and actress Sophia Bush offered young women a familiar piece of relationship advice: If you're questioning whether to leave your marriage because you fear you won't find someone better, the answer is always yes. Bush went further, suggesting that the fear of being too old or unreasonable for wanting more is a product of the patriarchy. Cooper built her brand largely by celebrating sexual experimentation, including encouraging young women to engage in highly explicit sexual experimentation early in dating. This is the same podcast Kamala Harris joined prior to the 2024 election, but I digress. RILEY GAINES FIRES BACK AT ALEX COOPER’S GRAPHIC DATING ADVICE: ‘IT IS NOT EMPOWERMENT. IT IS POISON’ Bush is now on her third marriage, with the first one lasting 5 months, the second lasting about a year, and the third to a woman. These are the voices our culture elevates as influential guides for young women. But enough about the who. Let's examine the what. The exchange reveals a worldview in which something better is always waiting. That personal and fleeting dissatisfaction is sufficient reason to abandon a commitment, and that the pursuit of more is interchangeable with empowerment. More what, exactly? More excitement? More affirmation? More freedom? Another relationship that will inevitably encounter the same imperfections as the last? At what point do we consider whether the relentless pursuit of more is precisely what leaves us feeling we have less? AMERICAN WOMEN HAVE BEEN LIED TO ABOUT MOTHERHOOD AND IT’S TIME TO FIX IT For decades, women have been sold a particular vision of liberation. Prioritize your career. Maximize your independence. Explore your sexuality without consequence. Reject marriage, delay motherhood, and never compromise your ambitions for someone else's needs. Above all, put yourself first. We were assured that freedom from traditional obligations would produce unprecedented happiness. TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND If that were true, we would certainly see it in society. But instead, what was promised as empowerment has delivered emptiness. Despite constant technological connectivity, loneliness and social isolation remain pervasive. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation are serious concerns, particularly among younger generations. These problems have many causes, and attributing them all to feminism would be intellectually dishonest. But ignoring the possibility that our prevailing philosophy has failed to deliver its promised fulfillment would be equally foolish. We’ve spent decades dismantling the institutions that tether individuals to one another, only to discover that autonomy is a poor substitute for belonging. Perhaps most tragically, we’ve taught women to regard sacrifice as oppression rather than an indispensable part of love. Consider the contradiction. A woman who sacrifices her time, energy, and health to climb the corporate ladder is celebrated as ambitious. A woman making comparable sacrifices for her husband and children is too often regarded as having surrendered her potential to the patriarchy. Why? ONE GROUP OF MARRIED AMERICANS IS HAVING MORE SEX — AND HAPPIER MARRIAGES I am profoundly grateful for the opportunities women have today. I’ve competed as a collegiate athlete, traveled the country, built a career, and achieved things my younger self could never have imagined. But no professional accolade, public recognition, or personal achievement has given me the satisfaction and purpose I’ve found in marriage and motherhood. They require more of me than anything I've ever done (even a 200-yard butterfly). It's hard. But "hard" and "bad" are not synonymous. Motherhood fundamentally changed my understanding of success. There's something remarkably clarifying about being needed by someone who has nothing to offer you in return except themselves. I don't view it as a limitation on my freedom, but instead a revelation of what my freedom is for. Which brings me back to Cooper, who just welcomed her first child with her husband. I genuinely congratulate her. But there's irony in continuing to promote perpetual self-prioritization through meaningless hookups and "girl-bossing" while building a life rooted in the very institutions modern feminism so often characterizes as oppressive. Perhaps motherhood will offer her the same perspective it offered me: that the deepest fulfillment isn't found in putting yourself first, but in loving someone enough to put them first. Of course, marriage and motherhood aren't the only paths to meaning. Women who are single, childless, or unable to have children are no less valuable. Purpose takes countless forms, but lasting meaning generally requires looking beyond ourselves. This is hardly a novel insight. Christianity has taught for centuries that a life centered exclusively on the self is ultimately impoverished. Love is not merely a feeling to be pursued while convenient. It is a commitment expressed through action, fidelity, humility, and sacrifice. Our culture treats these virtues as antiquated burdens, then wonders why so many feel unmoored. Cooper and Bush's advice is troubling because it reduces marriage to personal optimization. Marriage becomes less a covenant to honor than an arrangement to continually reassess against hypothetical alternatives. There are legitimate reasons marriages end, including abuse and betrayal. But reflexively encouraging people to search for something better without acknowledging the responsibilities of commitment isn't teaching empowerment like the self-proclaimed feminists like to claim. It teaches disposability. A generation encouraged to keep every option open may eventually discover that life's most meaningful commitments require closing certain doors. Choosing a spouse. Raising children. Building a family. Practicing faith. Serving a community. Creating something that will endure long after your own ambitions have faded. Like everything associated with risk, these commitments impose limits, but I’ve found they also give life its depth. Women deserve more than the hollow assurance that happiness is perpetually waiting in the next relationship, promotion, or reinvention of themselves. They deserve to know that fulfillment isn't always found in acquiring more and finding someone that validates your every desire. Often, it's found in giving more. The great lie of modern empowerment isn't that women are capable of extraordinary things. It's that a life devoted primarily to ourselves is the most extraordinary thing we can aspire to. articles.title: In 2018, Vanessa Hudgens bought a 1922 Los Angeles home from Gary Oldman for nearly $5 million; after restoring its kitchen and primary suite, she sold the historic estate to Ronan Farrow for $6.7 million in 2022
articles.summary: In 2018, actor Vanessa Hudgens bought a historic Los Angeles home previously owned by Gary Oldman for nearly $5 million.
articles.body: In 2018, actor Vanessa Hudgens bought a historic Los Angeles home previously owned by Gary Oldman for nearly $5 million. Built in 1922, the Georgian Colonial-style property had ivy-covered walls, mature trees and architectural details that reflected its old Hollywood history. Four years later, after renovating its kitchen and primary suite and adding her own design touches, Hudgens sold the house to journalist Ronan Farrow and his then-partner, Jon Lovett, for $6.725 million.As reported by OK! Magazine, the sale was completed on February 15, 2022. The property, located in the Los Feliz neighbourhood of Los Angeles, measured 3,168 square feet and had three bedrooms, four bathrooms and a separate guesthouse. The reported sale price was about $1.7 million more than the amount Hudgens and her then-boyfriend, actor Austin Butler, had paid for it in 2018.A historic house that attracted HudgensThe house, known as the Little DeMille, was reportedly built in 1922 by filmmaker Cecil B. DeMille. Before Hudgens bought it, the property belonged to actor Gary Oldman, who had acquired it in 2011 for just under $2.9 million, according to Architectural Digest. Hudgens told Architectural Digest that she had spent five years looking for a home before finding the property. Its greenery and historic character were central to its appeal.She was also drawn to the details that gave the house its character. “To me, there’s something so romantic about that, a home with character and quirks. I love the old Hollywood elements: The Art Deco air vents, the chandelier over the staircase, the yard that feels like a park,” she told Architectural Digest. Oldman had installed 18th-century French oak floors in the house, another feature that appealed to Hudgens. The property’s nearly half-acre grounds, mature gardens, terraces and citrus trees added to its appeal.How Hudgens changed the interiorsHudgens hired interior designer Jake Arnold to remodel the primary suite, a project that involved moving the bathroom and knocking down walls. She wanted the changes to suit her needs without erasing the house’s history. She handled the kitchen renovation herself during the pandemic. The work included new Carrara marble, painted cabinets, updated knobs and drawer pulls, and large oak beams that created open shelving. Extra tiles from the primary bathroom were reused as a kitchen backsplash.She also changed the breakfast nook, adding patterned wallpaper, a German pendant light from the 1950s and a leather banquette. The living room moved away from the white, monochromatic look she had initially planned. Instead, she chose a pink mohair sofa and green armchairs, along with vintage and antique pieces collected from shops she liked. Outside, Hudgens commissioned artist Carly Kuhn to paint a mural of faces around the pool. The garden had grapefruit and avocado trees, while the outdoor dining area was used for meals with friends.The sale to Ronan FarrowBy February 2022, Hudgens had sold the house to Farrow, the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and author of 'Catch and Kill,' and Lovett, a podcast host and co-founder of Crooked Media. As reported by OK! Magazine, the purchase price as $6,725,000. The property’s sale price was around 34% higher than the nearly $5 million Hudgens paid in 2018.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

Under oath, Alhallaq verbally confirmed his answers to both questions as “no,” matching those he initially submitted by mail. articles.title: SMX champion Levi Kitchen opens up about rebuilding confidence after frightening Daytona crash
articles.summary: Levi Kitchen reveals how a violent Daytona Supercross crash shattered his confidence and the mental battle he fought to win the 250SMX World Championship.
articles.body: Levi Kitchen is on top of the SuperMotocross world. But getting there required more than recovering from a serious injury. He had to learn to trust himself again. The 25-year-old Monster Energy Pro Circuit Kawasaki rider captured the 2026 Monster Energy SMX 250 Class World Championship in September 2026, securing his first professional title and ending a seven-year championship drought for his team. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS It was a career-defining moment for Kitchen, who had spent years coming close to winning a championship while battling injuries and setbacks along the way. "It was unreal," Kitchen told OutKick OutDoors in an exclusive interview. "I've had some heartbreaks, obviously been close, but it felt really good." "It was pretty emotional for me just because it had taken a while to win anything of that caliber," he added. But the road to that championship was anything but smooth. The long road back from Daytona In March 2025, Kitchen suffered a violent crash during the Daytona Supercross that left him with a broken collarbone and fractures in his upper back. The injuries sidelined him for the remainder of the Supercross season. And while he eventually healed enough to return to racing, Kitchen said the mental recovery was a different battle entirely. "Oh yeah, big time," he said when asked whether it was difficult to regain his confidence after the crash. "If I look back at that season, even when I came back on the bike, in 2025, I was maybe a top-five guy outdoors. And then at least was able to compete for the championship this year." Watch Levi Kitchen's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here: That progression didn't happen overnight. "Slowly but surely, I've made really good progress, and I have all my confidence back," Kitchen said. "It just goes to show, I think fans, or just anybody, don't realize how much injuries can really affect everything." "It can be a real pain in the butt to build yourself back up." For fans watching from the sidelines, a rider's return to competition might signal that the recovery process is complete. But as Kitchen explained, getting back on the bike doesn't necessarily mean getting back to the same level of confidence and performance. It took time, patience and a different approach to racing. Learning when to back off Looking back on everything he's experienced, Kitchen believes one of his biggest improvements has come from learning to trust his abilities while also recognizing his limits. "The biggest thing I would say is just finally the belief," he said. "The belief side of it is super important. And I think on any given day, if I show up with the belief that I can get something done, normally I can get it done." SUPERMOTOCROSS CHAMPION LEVI KITCHEN WANTS TO TRY TOURNAMENT BASS FISHING WHEN HE HANGS UP HIS HELMET But confidence alone wasn't enough. Kitchen also had to develop a little more restraint — something that doesn't always come naturally in a sport where riders are constantly pushing the limits of speed and control. "Just maturity of racing," he explained. "Now, if I don't really have it on a day, I try to be as smart as I can. Where before, I would probably still try and then end up on the ground or something." It's a lesson learned the hard way, but one Kitchen believes will serve him well beyond a single championship season. "I want to race for a lot more years to come and can't be too stupid," he said. That shift in mentality paid off in September when Kitchen secured the 250SMX World Championship at Thunder Ridge Nature Arena in Ridgedale, Mo. And the victory meant something special beyond his own accomplishments. Kitchen's title ended a seven-year championship drought for Monster Energy Pro Circuit Kawasaki, one of the most decorated organizations in 250-class racing. "Mitch has done so much for me," Kitchen said, referring to team owner Mitch Payton. "Me and Mitch have gotten close over the years, and he's been a great boss and friend of mine now. So it was super special." One championship down, but plenty more to chase Despite finally capturing that elusive first title, Kitchen insists he isn't suddenly feeling satisfied. In fact, winning the championship has only strengthened his belief in what he's capable of accomplishing. "It didn't really take any pressure off," he said. "The only thing it did was help me with the belief side of things. Just being able to execute." Kitchen has his sights set on both a Supercross and a Pro Motocross championship in 2027, and he plans to remain in the 250 class for at least another season. "The Supercross Championship has been a major goal of mine, so that's my first goal," he said. "But overall, just maybe be a little better than I was this year." And while the first championship was certainly worth celebrating, Kitchen knows there's no guarantee the next one will come any easier. "I don't think you'll ever be satisfied, really, which is a tough thing," he said. For now, though, Kitchen can take some satisfaction in knowing how far he's come. A year ago, he was still working to rebuild his confidence after a frightening crash. Now, he's a world champion. articles.title: Florida cop accused of stealing dead man's identity and moving into his home
articles.summary: Authorities uncovered the plot when the man's heirs tried to sell the south Florida home
articles.body:
A Florida police officer has been accused of stealing the identity of a man he found dead during a welfare check call and then moving into his home, authorities say.

Brian Louis Sguros, 35, a police officer in Lauderhill, Florida, was arrested this week by the Broward County Sheriff's Office.

Investigators allege he impersonated the deceased man, Dennis West, moved into the house he found West dead in, and then renovated the two-story south Florida home. Police say he lived there for years undetected.

Sguros has not commented on the charges. It's unclear whether he has legal representation yet. He has been placed on administrative leave from the Lauderhill Police Department.

In 2022, police were called to check on a 71-year-old resident of Lauderhill, Florida, Dennis West.

Officer Brian Louis Sguros was called in as back-up for the welfare check. When he found West dead of natural causes, he allegedly "created a complex scheme to take control of the individual's home," the Broward County Sheriff's Office said in a news release.

Investigators say Sguros told the medical examiner's office he was West's friend, though authorities found no indication the two knew each other, according to the news release. Court documents detail that the officer appeared in body cam footage during the welfare check and did not appear to have a prior relationship with the man.

He also allegedly told the county medical examiner that West had no living relatives, which authorities say say was also untrue, the release states.

Sguros then had West's body cremated, according to the BBC's news partner CBS.

According to a joint investigation by the sheriff's office and the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office, Sguros took possession of the home in August 2022 and moved in.

Authorities say in 2025, he allegedly filed paperwork with the property appraiser's office stating that his possession dated to August 2022.

Sguros said he took possession of the home because it was hazardous, and he wanted to prevent people from squatting, according to court documents.

He paid utility accounts which were in the deceased man's name. He also applied for a permit to replace exterior doors and windows, at the cost of $8,000 (£5970), according to court documents.

Sguros claimed he has increased the property's value, spending more than $214,000 (£159,717) on the home, according to the sheriff's office.

Sguros faces charges of official misconduct, criminal use of a deceased person's identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.

He was released from jail on a $25,000 bond.

Local law enforcement were made aware of the situation when West's heirs tried to sell the property, according a police affidavit.

Once Sguros eventually returned the keys to the property's rightful owners, he allegedly demanded reimbursement for improvements he had made to the property, court documents state.

The Lauderhill Police Department told BBC News that Sguros has been relieved of his duty and was placed on administrative leave with pay.

articles.title: In a Utah town, wild turkeys grew from a small flock to as many as 100 birds; after residents reported destruction around homes, the county moved to ban feeding them
articles.summary: Wild turkeys in Mendon, Utah, have grown from a flock of around a dozen birds to as many as 100, prompting concerns over damage to residential properties
articles.body: Wild turkeys in Mendon, Utah, have grown from a flock of around a dozen birds to as many as 100, prompting concerns over damage to residential properties and the continued feeding of wildlife. According to Utah Public Radio, the birds arrive from nearby mountains every winter, damaging trees, bushes and outdoor decorations as their numbers increase. In response, the Cache County Council unanimously approved an ordinance on 12 May 2026 banning the intentional or knowing feeding of wildlife on unincorporated county land. The rules introduce warnings and potential penalties for repeat offenders, while wildlife officials have highlighted public safety and disease risks associated with feeding wild animals.Why did wild turkeys cause damage around homes in a Utah townThe increasing number of wild turkeys has been associated with damage to trees, bushes and outdoor decorations. Buist described the problems residents faced as the flock expanded, explaining that the birds were large enough to break branches from trees and damage bushes. Decorative wreaths were also affected, with artificial berries being removed and the wreaths sometimes ruined.Buist also highlighted the mess left behind by the birds, referring to their droppings as another source of frustration for residents. Despite these problems, some people continued to feed the turkeys and other wildlife. The mayor said that feeding had become an ongoing issue for certain residents, particularly as the birds continued to gather in the area.Cache County approve a ban on feeding wild turkeys in MendonThe concerns in Mendon contributed to Cache County's decision to introduce restrictions on feeding wild animals. County policy analyst Andrew Erickson said the proposal originally came from the county sheriff, who had raised concerns about the excessive number of wild turkeys in Mendon and the fact that people were feeding them.The Cache County Council unanimously approved the ordinance during its 12 May 2026 meeting. The measure prohibits people from intentionally or knowingly feeding wildlife on unincorporated county land, including parcels between Mendon and the nearby Wellsville Mountains. The rules include exemptions for people feeding certain birds, farmers distributing feed to livestock and other specified circumstances.What penalties can residents face for violating Utah’s wild animal feeding banThe ordinance establishes a graduated enforcement process for people who violate the feeding restrictions. For a first offence, a person may receive a verbal warning and be given 48 hours to remove food from places where wild animals can access it. A subsequent offence within one year may result in an infraction.Further violations can carry more serious consequences. According to the report, people who receive three citations within 12 months, or who continue feeding wild animals for more than 30 days after being instructed to stop, could face a Class B misdemeanour. In Utah, infractions can carry fines of up to $750, while Class B misdemeanours can result in fines of up to $1,000 and up to six months in jail. Interim Cache County Attorney Dane Murray said the enforcement approach was not intended to criminalise otherwise law-abiding residents and welcomed the opportunity for an initial warning.Utah discourage feeding wild turkeys near residential areasThe Utah Division of Wildlife Resources has also highlighted the potential consequences of feeding wild animals. Faith Jolley, a spokesperson for the division, explained that animals fed by people often return to the same locations and may move closer to highways, towns and residential neighbourhoods. This behaviour can create public safety concerns as wildlife becomes accustomed to finding food near people.Jolley also described feeding turkeys as “highly discouraged”, citing the potential spread of diseases and the risk of harm when birds consume unfamiliar foods. These concerns formed part of the broader context surrounding the county's decision to restrict wildlife feeding. For Mendon Mayor Ed Buist, the new ordinance represents a response to the difficulties residents have experienced as the local turkey population has increased.You use AI every day.
